analysis.title: Weekly Economics, Thoughts of the Week: The Federal Reserve Is Expected to Increase Rates in December (November 20, 2026)
key_insights: Markets are pricing a 25bp Fed hike in December. Raymond James expects the hike and then a pause to let the cumulative effect of recent hikes work through the economy.

Some Fed officials have discussed a 50bp December hike and others up to 100bp of hikes by mid-2027. Raymond James calls these discussions premature and expects markets and the Fed to move toward its own, less aggressive path.

The report argues that rate expectations can shift quickly. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack was described as one of the more outspoken hawks on the FOMC in the October 16, 2026 edition and now sounds more moderate than many colleagues.

Raymond James says current inflation bears little resemblance to the post-pandemic surge, so the risk of a repeat of that episode remains low, even though inflation has been above target for an extended period.
Housing remains under strain. Existing home sales fell to levels not seen since the Great Recession, the median existing home price rose only 0.4% y/y, and the NAHB index fell to a 14-year low.

Residential improvements, which are nearly 40% of residential construction activity, are falling at the fastest y/y pace since January 2019. They had been offsetting weakness in single-family construction while multifamily stayed flat.

Housing starts rose 9.9% m/m in October to a 1.309 million annual rate, driven by multifamily (5+ units up 25.5% m/m). Permits fell 7.4% to 1.295 million, the lowest since May 2020, and were weak across home types and nearly all regions.

Pending Home Sales fell 4.7% m/m and 16.7% y/y in October to a record low, with no region improving. NAR's chief economist said October could be the low point as mortgage rates appear to have topped out, but Raymond James is less sanguine and expects further deterioration while rates stay at current levels or rise.

Raymond James expects housing weakness to stay short of a broader crisis but to keep pressuring home prices in 2027, especially new homes, and to reinforce the recession already underway in residential investment.

October retail sales rose 0.2% (in line with estimates) after 0.8% in September. Control group sales rose 0.6% and September's control group figure was revised up to 0.5% from 0.1%, which Raymond James reads as stable consumer demand.

October import prices rose 1.1% m/m, more than expected, and import prices excluding food and fuel rose 0.9%, the fastest monthly pace in six months. Raymond James says this adds to evidence of broadening price pressures after the CPI and PPI releases and supports its December hike expectation.

October industrial production fell 0.4% against an estimate of +0.2%, but utilities output fell 4.3% while manufacturing rose 0.3% and business equipment output rose 1.0% m/m and 7.8% y/y. Capacity utilization slipped to 76.4% from 76.8%.

The Conference Board LEI fell 0.3% in October, pulled down by consumer expectations and building permits. The Conference Board describes growth as increasingly investment-led with softer household demand, and forecasts 2.3% real GDP growth in 2026 and 2.1% in 2027.

Business inventories rose 0.5% m/m in September, in line with expectations, and the inventories-to-sales ratio fell to 1.33 from 1.42 a year earlier. Raymond James says this supports production but could widen the trade deficit as restocking draws on imports.

sector_views.rationale: Raymond James remains negative on the new home market for the rest of this year and into next, citing elevated mortgage rates near 7.5%, high construction costs, and a record-low Pending Home Sales Index. It expects further downward pressure on home prices in 2027.

macro_indicators.reading: 25bp hike expected by markets and by Raymond James, followed by a pause
macro_indicators.interpretation: Hike expectations are supported by broadening price pressures. Raymond James expects the Fed to pause after December and expects market pricing of further hikes into 2027 to moderate.

macro_indicators.indicator: Fed funds rate, path suggested by some Fed officials
macro_indicators.reading: 50bp in December, up to 100bp of hikes by mid-2027
macro_indicators.interpretation: Raymond James views these discussions as premature and a risk to the market narrative rather than its base case.

macro_indicators.reading: +0.2% m/m in October (in line with estimates), +6.8% y/y, after +0.8% in September
macro_indicators.interpretation: Headline held down by autos (-1.6%) and furniture (-2.3%), and kept from being weaker by a 1.5% rise at gas stations.
Stronger than the headline, and with the upward revision to September, it points to stable consumer demand.

macro_indicators.reading: +1.1% m/m in October, more than expected
macro_indicators.interpretation: Adds to the broadening price pressure evidence seen in CPI and PPI and reinforces the December hike expectation. No y/y rates were published because October 2025 survey data were not collected.

macro_indicators.indicator: Import prices excluding food and fuel
macro_indicators.interpretation: Fastest monthly pace in six months, pointing to non-fuel price pressure.
Agricultural export prices rose 1.2% and non-agricultural 1.1%.

macro_indicators.reading: -0.4% m/m in October versus an estimate of +0.2%, after +0.7% in September
macro_indicators.interpretation: The miss was driven by utilities (-4.3%). Manufacturing was up 0.3% and business equipment up 1.0%, so details are better than the headline.
Decline was driven mostly by lower utilities capacity use.

macro_indicators.reading: 25 in November versus 29 in October, lower than expected
macro_indicators.interpretation: Lowest since April 2012 per the release text. All components fell and 46% of builders cut prices, the highest share in 2020-2026.

macro_indicators.reading: 1.309 million SAAR in October, +9.9% m/m, +2.8% y/y, stronger than expected
macro_indicators.interpretation: Boosted by multifamily. Single-family starts rose 4.0% m/m but were down 3.2% y/y. Raymond James says the rise is not enough to end the slump.

macro_indicators.reading: 1.295 million SAAR in October, -7.4% m/m, -8.7% y/y, lower than expected
macro_indicators.interpretation: Lowest level since May 2020 and a weak signal for future construction.

macro_indicators.reading: -4.7% m/m and -16.7% y/y in October, lower than expected, a record low
macro_indicators.interpretation: Leads existing home sales by one to two months, so Q4 closings are expected to be sluggish.

macro_indicators.reading: -0.3% in October after unchanged in September, lower than expected
macro_indicators.interpretation: Dragged by consumer expectations and building permits, while all financial components were positive.

macro_indicators.reading: +0.5% m/m and +5.1% y/y in September, in line with expectations
macro_indicators.interpretation: Sales rose 1.8% m/m and the inventories-to-sales ratio fell to 1.33 from 1.42 a year earlier.

macro_indicators.reading: Raymond James 2.4% for full-year 2026 and 2.3% for 2027. Conference Board 2.3% for 2026 and 2.1% for 2027
macro_indicators.interpretation: Both sources expect continued expansion, with the Conference Board describing it as increasingly investment-led.
Keeps pressure on housing demand and builder sentiment.

risk_factors: Broadening price pressures (CPI, PPI, import prices) could push the Fed beyond a single December hike.
Some Fed officials have discussed a 50bp December hike and up to 100bp of hikes by mid-2027.
Elevated mortgage rates, high construction costs and still-expensive home prices could deepen housing weakness and pressure home prices in 2027.
Weakening building permits point to a thinner pipeline of future residential construction.
Softer household demand and falling consumer expectations, as shown in the LEI, could reduce the consumer's contribution to growth.
Business inventory restocking could widen the trade deficit through higher imports.
charts_described: Chart of residential improvements construction spending (year-over-year percentage change). The text states the category had grown strongly through Q1 2026 and is now declining at the fastest y/y pace since January 2019.
vol_and_positioning: Market pricing as shown in a CME-sourced chart (data as of 11/20/2026) tracks the number of 25bp hikes priced into the target policy rate upper bound across FOMC meetings from December 2026 through April 2027. The report text states that markets expect a December hike and increasingly expect the Fed to stay aggressive well into 2027.

tension_points.bull_case: Raymond James expects a 25bp December hike followed by a pause, with market and Fed expectations moderating toward its view. It argues the current inflation drivers differ from the post-pandemic surge, and that housing weakness acts as a drag on growth and inflation.
tension_points.bear_case: Markets are increasingly convinced the Fed must stay aggressive well into 2027. Some officials have discussed 50bp in December or 100bp by mid-2027, and CPI, PPI and import prices point to broadening price pressures.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Continued broadening of price pressures in upcoming inflation data, or officials moving from discussion to a larger December hike or hikes beyond December, would undercut the pause view. The report does not give a specific level.

tension_points.bull_case: NAR's chief economist said October could mark the low point in contract signings as mortgage rates appear to have topped out. NAR also pointed to a build-up of potential future demand.
tension_points.bear_case: Raymond James expects further deterioration as long as mortgage rates stay at current levels or rise. It cites record-low pending sales, six-year-low permits and a 14-year-low NAHB index.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Mortgage rates staying near ~7.5% or rising further would invalidate the NAR bottoming view, per Raymond James.

theme_stances.key_argument: The Fed should hike 25bp in December and then pause, and talk of 50bp or 100bp more is premature.
Housing remains one of the clearest areas of weakness and should keep acting as a drag on growth and inflation.
theme_stances.evidence: housing remains one of the clearest areas of economic weakness
